title: The gods and demons and the breath (1.3)
hook: the gods audition every sense to sing their victory chant, and only the plain breath can't be corrupted
tomorrow: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashanaya: at first there was nothing, covered by death, which is hunger. Your line was from hunger, the world.

Lead me from the unreal to the real. From darkness to light. From death to the deathless. It's chanted in Sanskrit before classes, pujas, yoga sessions, school assemblies. And it comes from today's chapter of the Brihadaranyaka, at the end of a strange little war story. The gods and the demons, both children of the creator Prajapati, are fighting over the worlds. The gods' plan: win with a chant. All they need is a singer the demons can't corrupt. So they start auditioning the parts of the body.
screen: `LEAD ME FROM THE UNREAL TO THE REAL.` → `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?` → `THE GODS NEED A SINGER.`

segments.voice: First they ask speech. Speech sings for them, but keeps the best part for itself: the pleasure of speaking well. The demons rush at it and pierce it with evil. That, says the text, is why we say things we shouldn't. Then smell. Then the eye. Then the ear. Then the mind. Each one sings, keeps something back, and gets pierced. That's why we see, hear and think things we wish we hadn't. Last, the gods turn to the breath in the mouth, the plain breath that keeps you alive. Breath sings. The demons rush at it too, and they shatter, the text says, like a clod of earth thrown against a stone. Why breath? One common reading: it took nothing for itself. It sang for everyone. A few weeks ago, the Chandogya told this same battle in a few lines, and its longer story had breath win by threatening to leave. Here the battle is told in full, and on this reading breath wins because it's the one faculty that doesn't grab. Then breath carries each of the others past death. Speech becomes fire. The eye becomes the sun. The ear becomes the directions. The mind becomes the moon. And the chapter ends with the chant: asato ma sad gamaya, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, mrityor ma amritam gamaya. The text explains its own words. The unreal is death; the real is the deathless. Darkness is death; light is the deathless. In its home, this chant is a prayer to be carried the way breath carries the senses.
screen: `SPEECH SINGS, AND KEEPS SOME FOR ITSELF.` · `EYE, EAR, MIND: EACH ONE PIERCED.` · `THE DEMONS SHATTER ON THE BREATH.` · `ASATO MA SAD GAMAYA.` · then, large: `BREATH IS UNTOUCHED BY EVIL.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move without steering it, and notice how it takes nothing for itself: it comes in, feeds every part of you, and goes. When a thought, a sound or a worry grabs you, let it be, and come back to the breath under it. If you pray, you can say the old chant silently on the out-breath: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless.
Prana, breath, the life-force. In this story prana is the one faculty the demons couldn't pierce, because it sang for everyone and kept nothing back.
Your line: breath is untouched by evil. Tomorrow, the first words ever spoken. Until then.

howItsDone: Many Hindus chant asato ma sad gamaya at the start of study, worship or a gathering, and teachers often explain its three lines as the movement from death to the deathless.

original.note: Sanskrit prāṇa: breath, the life-force. pra (forth) + an (to breathe).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old myth about gods fighting demons.
what it means: every sense that grabs something for itself can be corrupted. the breath, which only gives, can't be.
what a scholar hears: the chant asato ma sad gamaya is glossed by the text itself (1.3.28): unreal and darkness mean death, real and light mean the deathless.

chat.says: Where does 'lead me from the unreal to the real' actually come from?
options: A Brihadaranyaka story: the gods' chant, sung by the breath that kept nothing for itself.
It was written for modern yoga classes as an opening chant, not from old scripture.
A Gita verse where Krishna tells Arjuna to step from the battlefield into the light.
chat.meaning: It ends the Brihadaranyaka's story of the gods' singers: speech, eye, ear and mind were pierced, but the breath sang for everyone and couldn't be.

notes: The index word is the title's head cut mid-word ("The gods and demons and the breath"); kept exactly as the validator requires. Suggest the outline give this day a word such as prana.
Order of the senses in 1.3 (speech, smell/breath of the nose, eye, ear, mind) and that each kept the enjoyment for itself: summarized from 1.3.2–6; confirm.
Breath of the mouth named Ayasya Angirasa (1.3.8, 'essence of the limbs') was left out for length; the clod-against-stone image is 1.3.7.
Elements: speech to fire, nose-breath to wind, eye to sun, ear to the quarters, mind to moon (1.3.12–16); the script omits wind for brevity. Confirm.
The text's own gloss of the three lines (1.3.28) is paraphrased. Transliteration given without diacritics: asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya, mṛtyor mā'mṛtaṃ gamaya.

Reviewer edit: 'breath took nothing for itself' is an interpretation (the text contrasts the senses that kept the good part for themselves with the breath the demons could not pierce, 1.3.2–7), now framed as the usual reading; 'the most-sung prayer' softened to 'the best-known chant'.
Day 333 retold a senses-contest story under Chandogya 1.2; this script refers back to it only as 'the senses argued over who was greatest'.
